title: Min Stack
description: Brute force to optimized: an O(n) scan for getMin versus a parallel min stack that keeps the running minimum always immediately available.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the MINIMUM element, all in O(1) time. Implement the MinStack class: push(val) pushes a value; pop() removes the top element; top() gets the top element; getMin() retrieves the minimum element currently in the stack.

blocks.caption: A second "min stack" runs alongside the main one, recording the minimum among everything pushed so far at each level

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["getMin() must run in O(1), not O(n)","The minimum needs to be tracked and updated INCREMENTALLY as values are pushed and popped, rather than recomputed from scratch each time"],["Both push AND pop must remain O(1) as well","A SECOND, parallel stack recording \"the minimum so far at each level\" keeps everything synchronized automatically, without any extra scanning"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

A regular stack easily supports push, pop, and top in O(1), but naively finding the minimum requires scanning every element (O(n)); the challenge is maintaining constant-time access to the CURRENT minimum, even as elements are pushed and popped in any order.

blocks.title: Analogy: Keeping a Running "Lowest Score So Far" Sticky Note With Every New Entry
blocks.text: Imagine stacking sheets of paper with numbers on them, and wanting to instantly know the lowest number among all the sheets currently in the stack, at any point. One trick: whenever a new sheet is added, also attach a small sticky note recording "the lowest number seen so far, INCLUDING this new sheet." When a sheet (and its sticky note) is removed, the sticky note now exposed on the NEW top sheet is automatically still correct, since it was computed at the time IT was added.

blocks.caption: Popping both stacks together keeps the min stack perfectly synchronized: whatever is exposed after a pop is automatically the correct minimum for the remaining elements

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: push(-2), push(0), push(-3), getMin(), pop(), top(), getMin()

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operation","Main stack","Min stack","Result"],"rows":[["push(-2)","[-2]","[-2]","-"],["push(0)","[-2,0]","[-2,-2]","-"],["push(-3)","[-2,0,-3]","[-2,-2,-3]","-"],["getMin()","-","-","-3 (min stack's top)"],["pop()","[-2,0]","[-2,-2]","-"],["top()","-","-","0 (main stack's top)"],["getMin()","-","-","-2 (min stack's top, now correctly reflecting the remaining elements)"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before recomputing the minimum from scratch on every getMin() call (an O(n) operation, too slow for the O(1) requirement), notice that a SECOND stack, updated in lockstep with the main one, can track the running minimum incrementally.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every time a value is pushed, the NEW minimum (considering everything currently in the stack) is either the new value itself, or whatever the minimum was just before this push, whichever is smaller.

Observation 2: Recording this "minimum so far, at this level" alongside EVERY push (not just recomputing once) means the CURRENT minimum is always immediately available: it is simply whatever was recorded at the very top.

Observation 3: When popping, removing BOTH the main stack's top AND the min stack's top together keeps them perfectly synchronized: whatever min-stack value is now exposed on top is EXACTLY the correct minimum for the remaining elements, since it was computed and recorded at exactly that point in history.

Observation 4: This "parallel stack" trick avoids ever needing to rescan or search for the minimum, since it is always precomputed and immediately available at the top.
This is the parallel "min stack" technique: a second stack, updated in lockstep with the main one, always keeps the current minimum immediately available at its top.
6. Brute Force Solution
Use a single plain stack for all operations; for getMin(), scan the entire stack to find the smallest value each time it is called.
Step by step algorithm

items: push, pop, and top operate directly on a single plain stack, each in O(1).
getMin() scans every element currently in the stack, returning the smallest one found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: push, pop, and top are already optimal using a plain stack, requiring no changes.
getMin() is implemented the most straightforward way: scan everything, which correctly finds the minimum but is far too slow to meet the O(1) requirement.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly finds the minimum every time, since a full scan always finds the true smallest value.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for push/pop/top, but O(n) for getMin() (a full scan).
Space: O(n), for the stack.
Limitation: getMin()'s O(n) scan directly violates the problem's O(1) requirement for EVERY operation; a parallel min-tracking stack achieves O(1) getMin() as well.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rescans the whole stack for every getMin() call. Instead, maintain a SECOND stack alongside the main one, where each push also records "the minimum among everything currently in the stack, INCLUDING this new value." Popping removes from BOTH stacks together, keeping them perfectly synchronized, so the min stack's top is always immediately correct.

Maintain two stacks: the main stack (for actual values) and a min stack (for running minimums). On push(val): push val onto the main stack; compute the new minimum (val, or the min stack's current top if smaller) and push it onto the min stack. On pop(): pop both stacks together. top() reads the main stack's top. getMin() reads the min stack's top.
9. Optimized Solution
Maintain a parallel min stack, updated in lockstep with the main stack, keeping the current minimum always immediately available.
Dry run for push(-2), push(0), push(-3), getMin(), pop(), getMin()

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Every getMin() call returns the correct value in O(1), matching the expected sequence -3, -2.

codes.python:
class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []
        self.min_stack = []                                                 # min_stack[i] = the minimum among stack[0..i]

    def push(self, val):
        self.stack.append(val)
        current_min = val if not self.min_stack else min(self.min_stack[-1], val)
        self.min_stack.append(current_min)                                  # every push also records the min "so far, up to here"

    def pop(self):
        self.stack.pop()
        self.min_stack.pop()                                                # popping BOTH together keeps them perfectly in sync

    def top(self):
        return self.stack[-1]

    def get_min(self):
        return self.min_stack[-1]                                           # O(1): always just the top of min_stack


if __name__ == "__main__":
    ms = MinStack()
    ms.push(-2)
    ms.push(0)
    ms.push(-3)
    print(ms.get_min())
    ms.pop()
    print(ms.top())
    print(ms.get_min())

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for every operation: push, pop, top, and getMin.
Space: O(n), for the two parallel stacks (the min stack duplicates one integer per main-stack entry).
Why This Works

Each min-stack entry captures "the minimum among the main stack's contents AT THAT EXACT MOMENT," computed once and never needing recomputation. Because pop() removes from BOTH stacks together, the min stack's new top after a pop is EXACTLY the minimum that was correct at that earlier point in history, which is precisely the correct minimum for the elements still remaining, since nothing about those remaining elements has changed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A pushed value is smaller than the current minimum","The new min-stack entry becomes this new, smaller value"],["A pushed value is NOT smaller than the current minimum","The new min-stack entry simply repeats the existing minimum (unchanged)"],["A pop occurs","Both stacks lose their top together, automatically exposing the correct minimum for whatever remains"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Every single push (not just ones that set a new minimum) also pushes onto the min stack, keeping the two stacks always the SAME size, which is what makes synchronized popping correct.
The min stack repeating a value (rather than only storing NEW minimums) is essential: without it, popping past a "record-setting" minimum would lose track of what the minimum should revert to.
getMin() and top() are both simple O(1) top-of-stack reads, with no computation needed at query time.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

When a data structure needs O(1) access to a running AGGREGATE (like a minimum, maximum, or sum) that changes as elements are added and removed in stack order, maintaining a PARALLEL stack that records that aggregate at each push (and popping both together) achieves O(1) for every operation.
Common mistakes

items: Only pushing onto the min stack when a NEW minimum is set (rather than on every push), which desynchronizes the two stacks' sizes and breaks correctness after a pop.
Forgetting to pop from BOTH stacks together, leaving the min stack out of sync with the main stack's actual current contents.
Recomputing the minimum from scratch on every getMin() call, missing the O(1) incremental-tracking opportunity entirely.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly explaining WHY every push (not just record-setting ones) must also push onto the min stack demonstrates a clear understanding of exactly why the two stacks must stay perfectly synchronized in size.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Design a stack with O(1) access to its MINIMUM (or maximum)" points directly toward a parallel stack recording that running aggregate at every push.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you reduce the min stack's extra memory usage? Only push a NEW entry onto the min stack when the minimum actually changes, storing (value, count) pairs to still support correct popping, trading a bit of complexity for less duplicated storage.
How would you support getMax() as well as getMin()? Maintain a THIRD parallel stack, tracking the running maximum in exactly the same way.

How would this generalize to a queue instead of a stack (a "min queue")? This is notably harder, since a queue's FIFO removal order does not align as neatly with a simple parallel-stack approach; it typically requires a more involved technique using two stacks internally.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The foundational "parallel auxiliary stack tracks a running aggregate" pattern, a technique that generalizes to tracking other running properties (max, sum) alongside a stack's primary contents.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(1) push/pop/top, O(n) getMin; O(n) space.
Optimized (parallel min stack): O(1) for every operation; O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Parallel auxiliary stack tracking a running aggregate (minimum)
Core Idea: A second stack records the running minimum at every push, and is popped in lockstep with the main stack, keeping the current minimum always immediately available at O(1)
Time: O(1) for every operation
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: EVERY push (not just new-minimum ones) must also push onto the min stack, keeping both stacks the same size so synchronized popping stays correct
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Two stacks, always pushed/popped together; min stack's top = min(new value, previous min stack top)
